questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had more money, I will buy a new laptop.
If I have more money, I would buy a new laptop.
If I had more money, I would buy a new laptop.
If I would have more money, I would buy a new laptop.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I had more money, I would buy a new laptop.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If she had checked the price, she wouldn't overpay for the shoes.
If she checked the price, she wouldn't have overpaid for the shoes.
If she would have checked the price, she wouldn't have overpaid for the shoes.
If she had checked the price, she wouldn't have overpaid for the shoes.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If she had checked..., she wouldn't have overpaid...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This product is sold in over fifty countries.
This product sells in over fifty countries.
This product is selling in over fifty countries.
This product sell in over fifty countries.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is sold in over fifty countries.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The order cancelled due to a payment error.
The order was cancel due to a payment error.
The order is cancelled due to a payment error.
The order was cancelled due to a payment error.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was cancelled due to a payment error.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The shop assistant which helped me was very polite.
The shop assistant who helped me was very polite.
The shop assistant whom helped me was very polite.
The shop assistant, who helped me, was very polite but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The shop assistant who helped me...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This store which opened last year offers great discounts but.
This store, that opened last year, offers great discounts.
This store which opened last year, offers great discounts.
This store, which opened last year, offers great discounts.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'This store, which opened last year, offers great discounts.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That price can't to be right, it's far too low.
That price can't be right, it's far too low.
That price cann't be right, it's far too low.
That price can't being right, it's far too low.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' + base verb expresses a confident negative deduction: 'that price can't be right.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The store could being closed on public holidays.
The store could to be closed on public holidays.
The store coulds be closed on public holidays.
The store could be closed on public holidays.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the store could be closed.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've bought three pairs of shoes this month.
I've been buying three pairs of shoes this month.
I'm buying three pairs of shoes this month already.
I've buy three pairs of shoes this month.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've bought three pairs of shoes.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've saved money since six months.
I've been saving money for six months.
I'm saving money for six months already.
I've been save money for six months.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been saving... for six months.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have spent all my salary.")
options: He said that he has spent all his salary.
He said he have spent all his salary.
He said that he spent all his salary already.
He said that he had spent all his salary.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'he had spent all his salary.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "How much does this cost?")
options: She asked me how much did that cost.
She asked me how much that costs.
She asked me how much that cost.
She asked me how much does that cost.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'she asked me how much that cost.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to spend all my pocket money on sweets.
I use to spend all my pocket money on sweets.
I was used to spend all my pocket money on sweets.
I used to spending all my pocket money on sweets.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to spend all my pocket money on sweets.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I use to paying by card now.
I'm used to pay by card now.
I'm used paying to by card now.
I'm used to paying by card now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to paying by card.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Try the jacket on to before you buy it.
Try on the jacket before you buy it.
Try on to the jacket before you buy it.
Try the jacket before on you buy it.
questions.explanation: 'Try on' means 'put on clothes to see if they fit': 'try on the jacket.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I need to pay back the money I borrowed.
I need to pay the money back to I borrowed.
I need to pay back to the money I borrowed.
I need to pay the money I borrowed back to.
questions.explanation: 'Pay back' means 'return money that was borrowed': 'pay back the money.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite of the high price, she bought the dress.
Although the high price, she bought the dress.
Despite the price was high, she bought the dress.
Despite the high price, she bought the dress.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the high price, she bought the dress.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The shop raised its prices, as a result customers stopped buying.
As a result the shop raised its prices customers stopped buying.
The shop raised its prices. As a result, customers stopped buying.
The shop raised its prices as a result, customers stopped buying.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'The shop raised its prices. As a result, customers stopped buying.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have cash enough to pay for the taxi.
We don't have enough cash to pay for the taxi.
We don't have enough of cash to pay for the taxi.
We hasn't enough cash to pay for the taxi.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough cash.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My father is really worried of the rising prices.
My father is really worried about the rising prices.
My father is really worried for the rising prices.
My father is really worried at the rising prices.
questions.explanation: 'Worried about' + noun/gerund means 'concerned about something': 'worried about the rising prices.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to an online store's customer service you haven't contacted before?
options: Hiya,
Yo,
Dear Sir or Madam,
Hey there,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir or Madam,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a named store manager?
options: Later,
Best regards,
Cheers,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Best regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could refund my order.
I was wondering if you could to refund my order.
I was wondering could you refunding my order.
I wonder if you refund could my order.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could refund my order.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the customer.' and 'The customer's card was declined.'?
options: This is the customer which card was declined.
This is the customer's card who was declined.
This is the customer whose card was declined.
This is the customer who card was declined.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the customer whose card was declined.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have paid such a high price never before.
I have paid never such a high price before.
Never I have paid such a high price before.
I have never paid such a high price before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never paid such a price.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the item has been shipped?
I'd like to know, whether the item has been shipped.
I'd like to know whether has the item been shipped?
I'd like to know whether the item has been shipped.
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time tomorrow, I ___ for a new phone.
options: am shopping
will shop
shop
will be shopping
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be shopping'.

questions.question: By Friday, the shop ___ its whole stock.
options: sells
is selling
will sell
will have sold
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have sold'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly we compare prices secondly check finally purchase.
Finally compare the prices, firstly check, secondly make purchase.
Firstly, compare the prices. Secondly, check the reviews. Finally, make the purchase.
Secondly firstly compare prices, finally check reviews.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't spend all your savings, will you?
You wouldn't spend all your savings, do you?
You wouldn't spend all your savings, would you?
You wouldn't spend all your savings, wouldn't you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't spend..., would you?'
